title: Review: Neutralisation and salts; Tests for ions; Group 7: halogens
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PT07#t1 term and clue written for the game; PT07#t3 term and clue written for the game; PT05#t4 term and clue written for the game; PT05#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AB04#N.15, PT05#N.7, PT07#N.12, AB04#N.4, PT05#N.11, PT07#N.6, AB04#N.10, PT05#N.3, PT07#N.14a, PT05#N.16, PT07#N.3. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Cation
items.clue: The positive particle in a salt, such as Ba²⁺.

items.label: Limewater
items.clue: Turns milky when CO₂ from a carbonate and dilute acid is bubbled in.

items.label: Bleach
items.clue: Solution of sodium chlorate(I), made from chlorine and cold dilute NaOH.

items.label: Oxidising agent
items.clue: Role of Cl₂ when it takes electrons from Br⁻ or I⁻ and is itself reduced.

questions.stem: Baking powder contains sodium hydrogencarbonate and a solid acid. When the cake batter gets wet, the two react. Why does the cake rise?

options.text: HCO₃⁻ accepts H⁺ from the acid, giving water and carbon dioxide gas.
The acid reacts with sodium, giving hydrogen gas.
A salt and water form, as in every neutralisation, and the steam lifts the cake.
HCO₃⁻ donates H⁺ to the acid, giving CO₃²⁻ and a gas.

questions.explanation: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂. The bubbles of CO₂ make the batter rise, just as CO₂ from a carbonate antacid makes you burp.

questions.stem: Bromine water is added separately to aqueous potassium chloride and to aqueous potassium iodide. Which observation is expected?

options.text: A reaction occurs with the potassium chloride only
There is no reaction with either of the two solutions
A reaction occurs with both of the salt solutions
A reaction occurs with the potassium iodide only

questions.explanation: Bromine oxidises iodide ions, which are below it in Group 7: Br₂(aq) + 2I⁻(aq) → 2Br⁻(aq) + I₂(aq), and the solution darkens to brown. Bromine cannot oxidise chloride ions.

questions.stem: A white solid gives a brick-red flame. Its solution fizzes with dilute hydrochloric acid, giving a gas that turns limewater milky. What is the solid?

options.text: Calcium carbonate
Lithium carbonate
Calcium sulfate
Sodium carbonate

questions.explanation: Brick-red is Ca²⁺; fizzing with a gas that turns limewater milky is CO₃²⁻.

questions.stem: Which reaction produces a salt and water, with no other product?

options.text: Potassium carbonate with hydrochloric acid
Ammonia with sulfuric acid
Barium hydroxide with nitric acid
Zinc with hydrochloric acid

questions.explanation: Each OH⁻ takes one H⁺ to form water: Ba(OH)₂ + 2HNO₃ → Ba(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O.

questions.stem: In which reaction is chlorine both oxidised and reduced?

options.text: Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO
Cl₂ + 2KBr → 2KCl + Br₂
H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl
2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl

questions.explanation: One Cl atom goes from 0 to −1 (reduced) in HCl; the other goes from 0 to +1 (oxidised) in HClO. That is disproportionation.

questions.stem: A student adds barium chloride solution to a solution of an unknown sodium salt, without adding acid first. A white precipitate forms. Why can the student not yet conclude that sulfate ions are present?

options.text: Barium chloride gives a white precipitate with every negative ion.
The white solid could be sodium chloride crystallising out of the mixture.
The solid could be barium carbonate, which acid would have prevented.
Barium ions react with water to form a white barium hydroxide precipitate.

questions.explanation: BaCO₃ is also white and insoluble. Dilute HCl first removes carbonate as CO₂, so a white precipitate after acidifying must be BaSO₄.

questions.stem: What are the parent acid and parent base of ammonium methanoate, HCOONH₄?

options.text: Parent acid HCOO⁻; parent base NH₄⁺
Parent acid HCOOH; parent base NH₄⁺
Parent acid NH₃; parent base HCOOH
Parent acid HCOOH; parent base NH₃

questions.explanation: The anion HCOO⁻ comes from methanoic acid; the cation NH₄⁺ formed when NH₃ accepted a proton. HCOOH + NH₃ → HCOONH₄.

questions.stem: At room temperature iodine is a solid but chlorine is a gas. Which statement explains this?

options.text: The I–I covalent bond is stronger than the Cl–Cl bond, so iodine molecules are harder to break up.
Iodine molecules have more electrons, so the London forces between them are stronger.
Iodine molecules are polar, so permanent dipole–dipole forces hold them together.
Iodine is more electronegative, so each molecule attracts its neighbours more strongly.

questions.explanation: I₂ has 106 electrons and Cl₂ has 34. Larger temporary dipoles form, so the intermolecular forces are stronger and more energy is needed to separate the molecules.

questions.stem: A garden-centre sack of white fertiliser crystals has lost its label. It could be ammonium sulfate, ammonium carbonate, ammonium chloride or potassium sulfate. Which pair of results shows it is ammonium sulfate?

options.text: Warming with NaOH(aq) gives a gas that turns damp red litmus blue; BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate that fizzes and dissolves when dilute HCl is added.
Warming with NaOH(aq) gives no alkaline gas; dilute HCl then BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate.
Warming with NaOH(aq) gives a gas that turns damp red litmus blue; dilute HCl then BaCl₂(aq) gives a white precipitate.
Warming with NaOH(aq) gives a gas that turns damp red litmus blue; dilute HNO₃ then AgNO₃(aq) gives a white precipitate.

questions.stem: Swimming pools are often disinfected by adding a white solid, Ca(ClO)₂, instead of chlorine gas. Why does it kill bacteria in the same way as chlorine does?

options.text: It releases chloride ions, which are toxic to bacteria even at low concentrations.
Its calcium ions are taken up by bacteria and stop their cells from dividing.
It gives chlorate(I) ions, the oxidising agent that chlorine forms in water.
It slowly releases chlorine gas, which kills the bacteria as it bubbles out.

questions.explanation: Ca(ClO)₂ is calcium chlorate(I). Dissolved, it gives ClO⁻ ions, which form HClO in water. These are the oxidising agents that kill bacteria, just as when Cl₂ reacts with water (Cl₂ + H₂O ⇌ HCl + HClO).

questions.stem: Which result shows that a solid contains ammonium ions?

options.text: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added; a gas forms that turns limewater milky.
It is warmed with NaOH(aq); a gas forms that turns damp red litmus paper blue.
NaOH(aq) is added to its solution; a white precipitate forms that stays on warming.
Its solution turns damp blue litmus paper red, and no gas forms on warming.

questions.explanation: OH⁻ ions remove H⁺ from NH₄⁺, releasing ammonia, the only common alkaline gas.
